It is Meccan.
Al-Qurtubi said: "This is the consensus."

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The surah of *Tabaraka* (al-Mulk) was revealed in Mecca."

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Durays, al-Hakim (who declared it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, a surah from the Book of Allah, consisting of only thirty verses, interceded for a man until he was forgiven: ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾." Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a hasan hadith."

Al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat*, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtarah* narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A surah in the Qur'an argued on behalf of its companion until it brought him into Paradise: ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾."

Al-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim (who declared it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, Ibn Nasr, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated from Ibn (p-1510) Abbas, who said: "One of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) pitched his tent over a grave, while he did not realize it was a grave. Suddenly, there was a person in the grave reciting the surah of al-Mulk until he finished it. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'It is the preventer, it is the saviour; it saves him from the punishment of the grave.'"

After narrating it, al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a gharib hadith from this route."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "*Tabaraka* is the preventer from the punishment of the grave." It was also narrated by al-Nasa'i, who declared it sahih, and by al-Hakim.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Rafi' ibn Khadij and Abu Hurayrah that they both heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The surah of *Tabaraka* was revealed to me; it consists of thirty verses, all at once, and it is the preventer in the graves."

Abd ibn Humayd in his *Musnad*, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said to a man: "Shall I present you with a hadith that will make you happy?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Recite ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾, and teach it to your family, all your children, the children of your household, and your neighbours. For it is the saviour, and it is the advocate that will argue before its Lord on the Day of Resurrection on behalf of its reciter, and it will seek for him that Allah save him from the Fire, and its companion will be saved by it from the punishment of the grave."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I would love for it to be in the heart of every person in my Ummah."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His statement: ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾. *Tabaraka* is a form of *tafa'ala* from *barakah*, and *barakah* means growth and increase. It was also said: [it means] He is exalted and magnified above the attributes of created beings. It was also said: [it means] He endures; He is the Everlasting, whose existence has no beginning and whose permanence has no end.

Al-Hasan said: *Tabaraka* means "He is sanctified." The form *tafa'ala* is for emphasis (*mubalaghah*). The hand is a metaphor for power and control. *Al-mulk* is the dominion of the heavens and the earth in this world and the Hereafter; He honours whom He wills and humiliates whom He wills, He raises whom He wills and lowers whom He wills. It was also said: the intended meaning of *al-mulk* is the dominion of prophethood. The first [interpretation] is better, because interpreting it generally is more praiseworthy and more eloquent in praise, and there is no basis for specifying it.

﴿And He is Able over all things﴾: that is, He is perfectly capable; nothing among things can overpower Him. He disposes of His dominion however He wills, whether by bestowing favour or by retribution, by raising or lowering, by giving or withholding.

﴿He who created death and life﴾. Death is the cutting of the connection of the soul to the body and its separation from it; life is the connection of the soul to the body and its attachment to it. It was also said: life is that by whose existence perception becomes valid. It was also said: life is that which makes a thing alive. It was also said: the intended meaning is death in this world and life in the Hereafter.

Death is mentioned before life because the original state of things is the absence of life, and life is an accident attached to them. It was also said: because death is closer to subjugation.

Muqatil said: ﴿He created death﴾ means the sperm-drop, the lump of flesh, and the clot of blood; and ﴿life﴾ means that He created him as a human and created the soul in him. It was also said: He created death in the form of a ram, which does not pass by anything without killing it, and He created life in the form of a horse, which does not pass by anything without giving it life. This was said by Muqatil and al-Kalbi.

It has come in the revelation: ﴿Say: The angel of death who has been assigned to you will take you [in death]﴾ [Surah al-Sajdah: 11]; and His statement: ﴿If you could see when the angels take the disbelievers in death﴾ [Surah al-Anfal: 50]; and His statement: ﴿Our messengers take him in death﴾; and His statement: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [Surah al-Zumar: 42]; and other verses besides these.

﴿That He may test you [to see] which of you is best in deed﴾: The lam is connected to *khalaqa* ("created"); that is, He created death and life in order to deal with you as one who tests you, [to see] which of you is best in deed, and then He will recompense you for that. It was also said: the meaning is: that He may test you, [to see] which of you remembers death most and is most fearful of it. It was also said: which of you is quickest to the obedience of Allah and most restrained from the prohibitions of Allah.

Al-Zajjaj said: the lam is connected to the creation of life, not to the creation of death.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' also said: His statement ﴿that He may test you﴾ does not govern ("fall upon") *ayyu* ("which"), because between the testing and *ayyu* there is an implied verb, as you say: "I tested you in order that I might see which of you is more obedient." Its like is His statement: ﴿Ask them which of them will vouch for that﴾ [Surah al-Qalam: 40], meaning: ask them, then look at which of them [will]. Thus *ayyukum* ("which of you") in the verse is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is *ahsan* ("best"), because an interrogative does not allow what precedes it to govern it.

The use of the comparative form, although the testing encompasses all their actions, which are divided into good and bad and not merely into good and better, is to announce that the primary and essential purpose of testing is the manifestation of the perfection of the goodness of the good-doers.

﴿He is the Mighty (al-'Aziz), i.e., the Overpowering who cannot be overpowered, the Forgiving (al-Ghafur) to whoever repents and turns back.﴾

﴿He who created seven heavens in layers﴾. The relative pronoun (*al-ladhi*) may be a follower of *al-'Aziz al-Ghafur*, either as an adjective (*na't*), as an explanatory apposition (*bayan*), or as a substitute (*badal*). It may also be disconnected from it, being the predicate of an omitted subject, or in the accusative as a praise (*mad*). *Tibaqan* ("in layers") is an attributive of "seven heavens", meaning: some of them above others. It is the plural of *tabaq* like *jabal* / *jibal* ("mountain / mountains"), or the plural of *tabaqah* like *rahbah* / *rihab* ("courtyard / courtyards"), or a verbal noun of *taabaqa*. It is said: *taabaqa*, *mutabaqah* and *tibaqan*. On this last view the attribute is a verbal noun for emphasis, or [the phrase is] with an omitted attributed noun, meaning: possessing layers. It may also be in the accusative as a verbal noun with an omitted verb, meaning: they were made into layers (*tubiqat tibaqan*).

﴿You will not see in the creation of the Most Gracious any discrepancy.﴾ This sentence is a second attribute of "seven heavens", or is a new sentence confirming what precedes it. The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone who is suitable for it. *Min* is additional, for emphasis of the negation.

The majority read ﴿min tafawut﴾ ("any discrepancy"). Ibn Mas'ud and his companions, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read *tafawut* (with *tashdid*, without an *alif*) — *tafawwut*. Both are two dialects, like *al-ta'ahhud* and *al-ta'hhud*, and *al-tahammul* and *al-tahammul*. The meaning according to both readings is: you will not see in the creation of the Most Gracious any contradiction, any disparity, any crookedness, or any inconsistency; rather, it is uniform, straight, and indicative of its Creator. Even though their forms and attributes differ, they agree in this respect.

﴿So return the gaze; do you see any rifts?﴾ *Futur* means cracks, fissures, and holes. That is: return your glance until that becomes clear to you by direct observation.

First He informed that there is no discrepancy in His creation; then He commanded, a second time, the repeated looking at that, for increased confirmation and the attainment of tranquillity.

Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: *al-futur* means cracks; it is the plural of *fatr*, which is a split.

Qatadah said: "Do you see any flaw?"

Al-Suddi said: "Do you see any holes?" Its root is from *tafattur* and *infitar*, which is splitting and cleaving. From it is the poet's saying:

*He built for you a sky without pillars, and adorned it, and there is no fissure in it.*

And the saying of another:

*You split the heart, then you returned to it your love, [so] the wound healed and the fissures closed up.*

﴿Then return the gaze twice﴾: that is, two returns, one time after another. Its accusative is as a verbal noun. The meaning of the dual is multiplication, as in *labbayka* and *sa'dayka* ("at Your service, again and again"). That is: a return after a return, however many times.

The rationale for commanding the repetition of looking in this manner is that one may not see the defect one thinks there is at the first glance, nor at the second.

For this reason He said first ﴿You will not see in the creation of the Most Gracious any discrepancy﴾, then said secondly ﴿So return the gaze﴾, then said thirdly ﴿Then return the gaze twice﴾. This is more eloquent in establishing the proof and more decisive in cutting off excuses.

﴿The gaze will return to you humbled (*khasi'an*)﴾: that is, the gaze will return to you humiliated and abased, [unable] to see anything of that. It was also said: the meaning of *khasi'an*: distanced, expelled from seeing any defect it sought. It is said: "I drove away the dog" (*khasa'tu al-kalb*), meaning: I distanced and expelled it.

The majority read *yanqalib* ("will return") with *jazm* (apocopation) as an answer to the imperative. Al-Kisa'i, in one transmission, read it with *raf'* (nominative) as a new sentence.

﴿While it is fatigued (*hasir*)﴾: that is, weary, exhausted. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, it has become tired before it sees any flaw in the sky. *Hasir* is a form like *fa'il* in the meaning of *fa'il* (active), from *husur*, which is exhaustion. It is said: "His sight became *hasar*, *yahsur*, *husur*," meaning: it became weary and ceased. From it is the poet's saying:

*I looked at her in al-Muhassab of Mina, and the glance returned to me while it was fatigued.*

﴿And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps﴾. After creating the heavens and their being free of defect and flaw, Allah, glorified is He, explained that He adorned it with this adornment, so that it became in the best creation, the most perfect form, and the most delightful shape. The bringing of the oath is to show the completeness of care. *Al-masabih* is the plural of *misbah*, which is a lamp. The stars were named lamps because they shine like the shining of a lamp. Although some stars are in other heavens above it, they appear as though they are all in the nearest heaven, because the bodies of the heavens do not prevent seeing what is above them of things that give light, since they are polished, transparent bodies.

﴿And We have made them as missiles against the devils﴾: that is, and We made the lamps into projectiles with which the devils are stoned. This is a second benefit, other than the first, which is their being an adornment for the nearest heaven. The meaning is that the devils who eavesdrop are stoned with them. *Rujum* is the plural of *rajm*, with a *fatha*, and it is originally a verbal noun used for the thing with which one is stoned, as in their saying: "The dirham is the minting of the amir" (i.e., the minted thing). It may also remain as a verbal noun, and an omitted attributed noun is understood, meaning: possessors of stoning. The verbal noun is pluralized in consideration of its types.

It was also said: the pronoun in His statement "and We have made them" refers to the lamps with an omitted attributed noun, meaning: their meteors, which are their fire kindled from them, not the lamps themselves, due to His statement: ﴿Except one who snatches away a snatch, and is pursued by a piercing flame﴾ [Surah al-Saffat: 10]. The reasoning behind this is that the lamps with which Allah adorned the nearest heaven do not vanish and are not used for stoning. Abu Ali al-Farisi said this in answer to one who asked him: "How can the lamps be an adornment when they are projectiles?" Al-Qushayri said: "Better than this view is to say: they are an adornment before the devils are stoned with them."

Qatadah said: Allah created the stars for three purposes: as an adornment for the sky, as projectiles against the devils, and as signs by which one is guided on land and sea. Whoever speaks about them other than this has spoken about what he does not know, transgressed, and wronged [himself]. It was also said: the meaning of the verse is: We made them into conjectures for the devils of mankind, who are the astrologers.

﴿And We have prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze﴾: that is, and We have prepared for the devils, in the Hereafter, after burning in this world with the meteors, the punishment of the Blaze, that is, the punishment of the Fire. *Al-sa'ir* is the most intense burning; it is said: "The fire was kindled (*su''irat*), so it is *mas'urah*" (blazing).

﴿And for those who disbelieve in their Lord﴾: from among the disbelievers of the children of Adam, or from among the disbelievers of both groups (humans and jinn). ﴿is the punishment of Hell.﴾ The majority read *'adhab* ("punishment") with *raf'* (nominative), as the subject, and its predicate is *lilladhina kafaru* ("for those who disbelieve"). Al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, and al-A'raj read it with *nasb* (accusative), in coordination with ﴿the punishment of the Blaze﴾.

﴿And wretched is the destination.﴾ That is, the place to which they will return, namely Hell.

﴿When they are thrown into it﴾: that is, cast into it, as firewood is cast into the fire. ﴿they will hear from it a roaring (*shahiq*)﴾: that is, a sound like the braying of donkeys at the first start of their bray, and it is the most hideous of sounds. His statement "*laha*" ("from it") is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*): that is, [a roaring] existing from it. This is because originally it was an attribute, and when it was placed first, it became a circumstantial.

Ata said: "al-Shahiq" is the groaning of the disbelievers when they are thrown into the Fire. The clause ﴿wa-hiya tafur﴾ (﴿while it boils﴾) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while it is boiling with them, boiling like the cauldron (mirjal). From this is the saying of Hassan:

"You left your cooking pot with nothing in it, / while the pot of the caravan is hot and boiling."

﴿Takadu tamayyazu min al-ghayz﴾ means: it nearly splits apart, some of it separating from the rest out of its rage against them.

Ibn Qutaybah said: "It nearly bursts with fury against the disbelievers."

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "tamayyazu" with a single, lightened tā', while the original form is "tatamayyazu" with two tā's.

Ṭalḥah read it with two tā's, in the original form.

al-Bazzi, from Ibn Kathir, read it with a shadda, by assimilating one of the two tā's into the other.

al-Ḍaḥḥak read "tamāyaza" with an alif and a single tā', the original being "tatamāyazu." Zayd ibn ʿAli read "tamīza," from māza yamīzu. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, or in the nominative position as another predicate of a subject.

The clause ﴿kullama ulqiya fīha fawjun saʾalahum khazanatuha﴾ (﴿Whenever a group is thrown into it, its keepers ask them﴾) is a resumed clause explaining the state of its inhabitants, or it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "tamayyazu." The fawj is a group of people; meaning: whenever a group of disbelievers is thrown into Hell, its keepers, the angels, ask them a question of rebuke and reproach: ﴿Did there not come to you﴾ in the world ﴿a warner who warned you of this day and cautioned you against it?﴾

The clause ﴿qalu bala qad jaʾana nadhir﴾ (﴿They said: "Yes, indeed, a warner came to us"﴾) is a resumed clause answering an implied question, as if it had been said: "What did they say after this question?" So He said: ﴿They said: "Yes, indeed, a warner came to us, who warned us, frightened us, and informed us of this day, but we denied that warner."﴾ ﴿And we said: "Allah has not sent down anything"﴾ of things ﴿upon the tongues of you﴾ ﴿"You are only in great error"﴾, meaning: in going astray from the truth and distance from what is right.

The meaning is that each of those groups, relating to the keepers of Hell what had been said to them by those sent to them, says: "You, O messengers, in what you claim, that Allah has sent down to you signs by which you warn us, you are only in a great going astray from the truth and distance from what is right, which cannot be measured."

Then He related another saying of theirs, spoken after that saying: ﴿And they said: "Had we been listening or reasoning, we would not have been among the companions of the blaze."﴾ Meaning: had we listened to what the messengers addressed us with, or reasoned about any of it, we would not have been counted among the people of the Fire, or among those punished by the blaze, who are the devils, as has passed.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Had we listened with the hearing of one who comprehends, or reasoned with the reason of one who discerns and considers, we would not have been among the people of the Fire."

When they confessed this confession, Allah, glory be to Him, said: ﴿So they acknowledged their sin﴾, which made them deserving of the punishment of the Fire, namely disbelief and denial of the prophets. ﴿So away with the companions of the blaze﴾, meaning: far away from them, from Allah and from His mercy.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr and Abu Salih said: "It is a valley in Hell called al-Suḥq."

The majority read ﴿fasuḥqan﴾ with a sukun on the ḥā'. al-Kisai and Abu Jaʿfar read it with a ḍamma, and both are dialectal forms, like al-suḥt and al-ruʿb.

Al-Zajjaj and Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: "Fasuḥqan" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: Allah made them far away with a distancing.

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: "The analogical form would have been isḥāqan, but the verbal noun came with deletion." The lam in ﴿li-aṣḥab al-saʿir﴾ is for specification (bayān), as in ﴿hayta laka﴾ (Yusuf: 23).

ʿAbd ibn Humayd related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding ﴿seven heavens in layers (ṭibaqan)﴾, that he said: "some of them above others."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, regarding ﴿You will not see in the creation of the Most Merciful any inconsistency (tafawut)﴾, that he said: "Not one part of it differing from another in a dividing difference."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related also from him, regarding ﴿inconsistency (tafawut)﴾, that he said: "cracking (tashaqquq)." And regarding ﴿Do you see any rifts (futur)?﴾, he said: "cracks (shuquq)." And regarding ﴿despised (khasi'an)﴾, he said: "humiliated (dhalilan)," ﴿and he is fatigued (haseer)﴾: "weary (kalil)."

Ibn Jarir also related from him:
He said: "al-futur is al-wahy (cracking, fissure)."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him also, regarding ﴿rifts (futur)﴾: "cracking or flaw." And regarding ﴿the sight will return to you﴾: "it will return to you, ﴿despised (khasi'an)﴾: "humbled (saghiran)," ﴿and he is fatigued (haseer)﴾: "exhausted (ma'yiyy), seeing nothing."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him: ﴿despised (khasi'an)﴾: "humiliated (dhalilan)," ﴿and he is fatigued (haseer)﴾: "exhausted, turned back (muratja')."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿takadu tamayyazu﴾: "it nearly separates (tatafarraqu)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related also from him, ﴿takadu tamayyazu﴾: "some of it parts from others."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related also from him, ﴿fasuḥqan﴾: "distance (bu'dan)."

It is Meccan.
Al-Qurtubi said: "This is the consensus."

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The surah of *Tabaraka* (al-Mulk) was revealed in Mecca."

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Durays, al-Hakim (who declared it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, a surah from the Book of Allah, consisting of only thirty verses, interceded for a man until he was forgiven: ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾." Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a hasan hadith."

Al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat*, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtarah* narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A surah in the Qur'an argued on behalf of its companion until it brought him into Paradise: ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾."

Al-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim (who declared it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, Ibn Nasr, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated from Ibn (p-1510) Abbas, who said: "One of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) pitched his tent over a grave, while he did not realize it was a grave. Suddenly, there was a person in the grave reciting the surah of al-Mulk until he finished it. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'It is the preventer, it is the saviour; it saves him from the punishment of the grave.'"

After narrating it, al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a gharib hadith from this route."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "*Tabaraka* is the preventer from the punishment of the grave." It was also narrated by al-Nasa'i, who declared it sahih, and by al-Hakim.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Rafi' ibn Khadij and Abu Hurayrah that they both heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The surah of *Tabaraka* was revealed to me; it consists of thirty verses, all at once, and it is the preventer in the graves."

Abd ibn Humayd in his *Musnad*, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said to a man: "Shall I present you with a hadith that will make you happy?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Recite ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾, and teach it to your family, all your children, the children of your household, and your neighbours. For it is the saviour, and it is the advocate that will argue before its Lord on the Day of Resurrection on behalf of its reciter, and it will seek for him that Allah save him from the Fire, and its companion will be saved by it from the punishment of the grave."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I would love for it to be in the heart of every person in my Ummah."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

It was also said: the intended meaning is death in this world and life in the Hereafter.

This was said by Muqatil and al-Kalbi.

It has come in the revelation: ﴿Say: The angel of death who has been assigned to you will take you [in death]﴾ [Surah al-Sajdah: 11]; and His statement: ﴿If you could see when the angels take the disbelievers in death﴾ [Surah al-Anfal: 50]; and His statement: ﴿Our messengers take him in death﴾; and His statement: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [Surah al-Zumar: 42]; and other verses besides these.

﴿That He may test you [to see] which of you is best in deed﴾: The lam is connected to *khalaqa* ("created"); that is, He created death and life in order to deal with you as one who tests you, [to see] which of you is best in deed, and then He will recompense you for that. It was also said: the meaning is: that He may test you, [to see] which of you remembers death most and is most fearful of it. It was also said: which of you is quickest to the obedience of Allah and most restrained from the prohibitions of Allah.

Al-Zajjaj said: the lam is connected to the creation of life, not to the creation of death.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' also said: His statement ﴿that He may test you﴾ does not govern ("fall upon") *ayyu* ("which"), because between the testing and *ayyu* there is an implied verb, as you say: "I tested you in order that I might see which of you is more obedient." Its like is His statement: ﴿Ask them which of them will vouch for that﴾ [Surah al-Qalam: 40], meaning: ask them, then look at which of them [will]. Thus *ayyukum* ("which of you") in the verse is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is *ahsan* ("best"), because an interrogative does not allow what precedes it to govern it.

The use of the comparative form, although the testing encompasses all their actions, which are divided into good and bad and not merely into good and better, is to announce that the primary and essential purpose of testing is the manifestation of the perfection of the goodness of the good-doers.

﴿He is the Mighty (al-'Aziz), i.e., the Overpowering who cannot be overpowered, the Forgiving (al-Ghafur) to whoever repents and turns back.﴾

﴿He who created seven heavens in layers﴾. The relative pronoun (*al-ladhi*) may be a follower of *al-'Aziz al-Ghafur*, either as an adjective (*na't*), as an explanatory apposition (*bayan*), or as a substitute (*badal*). It may also be disconnected from it, being the predicate of an omitted subject, or in the accusative as a praise (*mad*). *Tibaqan* ("in layers") is an attributive of "seven heavens", meaning: some of them above others. It is the plural of *tabaq* like *jabal* / *jibal* ("mountain / mountains"), or the plural of *tabaqah* like *rahbah* / *rihab* ("courtyard / courtyards"), or a verbal noun of *taabaqa*. It is said: *taabaqa*, *mutabaqah* and *tibaqan*. On this last view the attribute is a verbal noun for emphasis, or [the phrase is] with an omitted attributed noun, meaning: possessing layers. It may also be in the accusative as a verbal noun with an omitted verb, meaning: they were made into layers (*tubiqat tibaqan*).

﴿You will not see in the creation of the Most Gracious any discrepancy.﴾ This sentence is a second attribute of "seven heavens", or is a new sentence confirming what precedes it. The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone who is suitable for it. *Min* is additional, for emphasis of the negation.

The majority read ﴿min tafawut﴾ ("any discrepancy"). Ibn Mas'ud and his companions, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read *tafawut* (with *tashdid*, without an *alif*) — *tafawwut*. Both are two dialects, like *al-ta'ahhud* and *al-ta'hhud*, and *al-tahammul* and *al-tahammul*. The meaning according to both readings is: you will not see in the creation of the Most Gracious any contradiction, any disparity, any crookedness, or any inconsistency; rather, it is uniform, straight, and indicative of its Creator. Even though their forms and attributes differ, they agree in this respect.

﴿So return the gaze; do you see any rifts?﴾ *Futur* means cracks, fissures, and holes. That is: return your glance until that becomes clear to you by direct observation.

First He informed that there is no discrepancy in His creation; then He commanded, a second time, the repeated looking at that, for increased confirmation and the attainment of tranquillity.

Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: *al-futur* means cracks; it is the plural of *fatr*, which is a split.

Qatadah said: "Do you see any flaw?"

Al-Suddi said: "Do you see any holes?" Its root is from *tafattur* and *infitar*, which is splitting and cleaving. From it is the poet's saying:

*He built for you a sky without pillars, and adorned it, and there is no fissure in it.*

And the saying of another:

*You split the heart, then you returned to it your love, [so] the wound healed and the fissures closed up.*

﴿Then return the gaze twice﴾: that is, two returns, one time after another. Its accusative is as a verbal noun. The meaning of the dual is multiplication, as in *labbayka* and *sa'dayka* ("at Your service, again and again"). That is: a return after a return, however many times.

The rationale for commanding the repetition of looking in this manner is that one may not see the defect one thinks there is at the first glance, nor at the second.

For this reason He said first ﴿You will not see in the creation of the Most Gracious any discrepancy﴾, then said secondly ﴿So return the gaze﴾, then said thirdly ﴿Then return the gaze twice﴾. This is more eloquent in establishing the proof and more decisive in cutting off excuses.

﴿The gaze will return to you humbled (*khasi'an*)﴾: that is, the gaze will return to you humiliated and abased, [unable] to see anything of that. It was also said: the meaning of *khasi'an*: distanced, expelled from seeing any defect it sought. It is said: "I drove away the dog" (*khasa'tu al-kalb*), meaning: I distanced and expelled it.

The majority read *yanqalib* ("will return") with *jazm* (apocopation) as an answer to the imperative. Al-Kisa'i, in one transmission, read it with *raf'* (nominative) as a new sentence.

﴿While it is fatigued (*hasir*)﴾: that is, weary, exhausted. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, it has become tired before it sees any flaw in the sky. *Hasir* is a form like *fa'il* in the meaning of *fa'il* (active), from *husur*, which is exhaustion. It is said: "His sight became *hasar*, *yahsur*, *husur*," meaning: it became weary and ceased. From it is the poet's saying:

*I looked at her in al-Muhassab of Mina, and the glance returned to me while it was fatigued.*

﴿And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps﴾. After creating the heavens and their being free of defect and flaw, Allah, glorified is He, explained that He adorned it with this adornment, so that it became in the best creation, the most perfect form, and the most delightful shape. The bringing of the oath is to show the completeness of care. *Al-masabih* is the plural of *misbah*, which is a lamp. The stars were named lamps because they shine like the shining of a lamp. Although some stars are in other heavens above it, they appear as though they are all in the nearest heaven, because the bodies of the heavens do not prevent seeing what is above them of things that give light, since they are polished, transparent bodies.

﴿And We have made them as missiles against the devils﴾: that is, and We made the lamps into projectiles with which the devils are stoned. This is a second benefit, other than the first, which is their being an adornment for the nearest heaven. The meaning is that the devils who eavesdrop are stoned with them. *Rujum* is the plural of *rajm*, with a *fatha*, and it is originally a verbal noun used for the thing with which one is stoned, as in their saying: "The dirham is the minting of the amir" (i.e., the minted thing). It may also remain as a verbal noun, and an omitted attributed noun is understood, meaning: possessors of stoning. The verbal noun is pluralized in consideration of its types.

It was also said: the pronoun in His statement "and We have made them" refers to the lamps with an omitted attributed noun, meaning: their meteors, which are their fire kindled from them, not the lamps themselves, due to His statement: ﴿Except one who snatches away a snatch, and is pursued by a piercing flame﴾ [Surah al-Saffat: 10]. The reasoning behind this is that the lamps with which Allah adorned the nearest heaven do not vanish and are not used for stoning. Abu Ali al-Farisi said this in answer to one who asked him: "How can the lamps be an adornment when they are projectiles?" Al-Qushayri said: "Better than this view is to say: they are an adornment before the devils are stoned with them."

Qatadah said: Allah created the stars for three purposes: as an adornment for the sky, as projectiles against the devils, and as signs by which one is guided on land and sea. Whoever speaks about them other than this has spoken about what he does not know, transgressed, and wronged [himself]. It was also said: the meaning of the verse is: We made them into conjectures for the devils of mankind, who are the astrologers.

﴿And We have prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze﴾: that is, and We have prepared for the devils, in the Hereafter, after burning in this world with the meteors, the punishment of the Blaze, that is, the punishment of the Fire. *Al-sa'ir* is the most intense burning; it is said: "The fire was kindled (*su''irat*), so it is *mas'urah*" (blazing).

﴿And for those who disbelieve in their Lord﴾: from among the disbelievers of the children of Adam, or from among the disbelievers of both groups (humans and jinn). ﴿is the punishment of Hell.﴾ The majority read *'adhab* ("punishment") with *raf'* (nominative), as the subject, and its predicate is *lilladhina kafaru* ("for those who disbelieve"). Al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, and al-A'raj read it with *nasb* (accusative), in coordination with ﴿the punishment of the Blaze﴾.

﴿And wretched is the destination.﴾ That is, the place to which they will return, namely Hell.

﴿When they are thrown into it﴾: that is, cast into it, as firewood is cast into the fire. ﴿they will hear from it a roaring (*shahiq*)﴾: that is, a sound like the braying of donkeys at the first start of their bray, and it is the most hideous of sounds. His statement "*laha*" ("from it") is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*): that is, [a roaring] existing from it. This is because originally it was an attribute, and when it was placed first, it became a circumstantial.

Ata said: "al-Shahiq" is the groaning of the disbelievers when they are thrown into the Fire. The clause ﴿wa-hiya tafur﴾ (﴿while it boils﴾) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while it is boiling with them, boiling like the cauldron (mirjal). From this is the saying of Hassan:

"You left your cooking pot with nothing in it, / while the pot of the caravan is hot and boiling."

﴿Takadu tamayyazu min al-ghayz﴾ means: it nearly splits apart, some of it separating from the rest out of its rage against them.

Ibn Qutaybah said: "It nearly bursts with fury against the disbelievers."

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "tamayyazu" with a single, lightened tā', while the original form is "tatamayyazu" with two tā's.

Ṭalḥah read it with two tā's, in the original form.

al-Bazzi, from Ibn Kathir, read it with a shadda, by assimilating one of the two tā's into the other.

al-Ḍaḥḥak read "tamāyaza" with an alif and a single tā', the original being "tatamāyazu." Zayd ibn ʿAli read "tamīza," from māza yamīzu. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, or in the nominative position as another predicate of a subject.

The clause ﴿kullama ulqiya fīha fawjun saʾalahum khazanatuha﴾ (﴿Whenever a group is thrown into it, its keepers ask them﴾) is a resumed clause explaining the state of its inhabitants, or it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "tamayyazu." The fawj is a group of people; meaning: whenever a group of disbelievers is thrown into Hell, its keepers, the angels, ask them a question of rebuke and reproach: ﴿Did there not come to you﴾ in the world ﴿a warner who warned you of this day and cautioned you against it?﴾

The clause ﴿qalu bala qad jaʾana nadhir﴾ (﴿They said: "Yes, indeed, a warner came to us"﴾) is a resumed clause answering an implied question, as if it had been said: "What did they say after this question?" So He said: ﴿They said: "Yes, indeed, a warner came to us, who warned us, frightened us, and informed us of this day, but we denied that warner."﴾ ﴿And we said: "Allah has not sent down anything"﴾ of things ﴿upon the tongues of you﴾ ﴿"You are only in great error"﴾, meaning: in going astray from the truth and distance from what is right.

The meaning is that each of those groups, relating to the keepers of Hell what had been said to them by those sent to them, says: "You, O messengers, in what you claim, that Allah has sent down to you signs by which you warn us, you are only in a great going astray from the truth and distance from what is right, which cannot be measured."

Then He related another saying of theirs, spoken after that saying: ﴿And they said: "Had we been listening or reasoning, we would not have been among the companions of the blaze."﴾ Meaning: had we listened to what the messengers addressed us with, or reasoned about any of it, we would not have been counted among the people of the Fire, or among those punished by the blaze, who are the devils, as has passed.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Had we listened with the hearing of one who comprehends, or reasoned with the reason of one who discerns and considers, we would not have been among the people of the Fire."

When they confessed this confession, Allah, glory be to Him, said: ﴿So they acknowledged their sin﴾, which made them deserving of the punishment of the Fire, namely disbelief and denial of the prophets. ﴿So away with the companions of the blaze﴾, meaning: far away from them, from Allah and from His mercy.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr and Abu Salih said: "It is a valley in Hell called al-Suḥq."

The majority read ﴿fasuḥqan﴾ with a sukun on the ḥā'. al-Kisai and Abu Jaʿfar read it with a ḍamma, and both are dialectal forms, like al-suḥt and al-ruʿb.

Al-Zajjaj and Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: "Fasuḥqan" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: Allah made them far away with a distancing.

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: "The analogical form would have been isḥāqan, but the verbal noun came with deletion." The lam in ﴿li-aṣḥab al-saʿir﴾ is for specification (bayān), as in ﴿hayta laka﴾ (Yusuf: 23).

ʿAbd ibn Humayd related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding ﴿seven heavens in layers (ṭibaqan)﴾, that he said: "some of them above others."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, regarding ﴿You will not see in the creation of the Most Merciful any inconsistency (tafawut)﴾, that he said: "Not one part of it differing from another in a dividing difference."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related also from him, regarding ﴿inconsistency (tafawut)﴾, that he said: "cracking (tashaqquq)." And regarding ﴿Do you see any rifts (futur)?﴾, he said: "cracks (shuquq)." And regarding ﴿despised (khasi'an)﴾, he said: "humiliated (dhalilan)," ﴿and he is fatigued (haseer)﴾: "weary (kalil)."

Ibn Jarir also related from him:
He said: "al-futur is al-wahy (cracking, fissure)."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him also, regarding ﴿rifts (futur)﴾: "cracking or flaw." And regarding ﴿the sight will return to you﴾: "it will return to you, ﴿despised (khasi'an)﴾: "humbled (saghiran)," ﴿and he is fatigued (haseer)﴾: "exhausted (ma'yiyy), seeing nothing."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him: ﴿despised (khasi'an)﴾: "humiliated (dhalilan)," ﴿and he is fatigued (haseer)﴾: "exhausted, turned back (muratja')."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿takadu tamayyazu﴾: "it nearly separates (tatafarraqu)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related also from him, ﴿takadu tamayyazu﴾: "some of it parts from others."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related also from him, ﴿fasuḥqan﴾: "distance (bu'dan)."

It is Meccan.
Al-Qurtubi said: "This is the consensus."

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The surah of *Tabaraka* (al-Mulk) was revealed in Mecca."

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Durays, al-Hakim (who declared it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, a surah from the Book of Allah, consisting of only thirty verses, interceded for a man until he was forgiven: ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾." Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a hasan hadith."

Al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat*, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtarah* narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A surah in the Qur'an argued on behalf of its companion until it brought him into Paradise: ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾."

Al-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim (who declared it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, Ibn Nasr, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated from Ibn (p-1510) Abbas, who said: "One of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) pitched his tent over a grave, while he did not realize it was a grave. Suddenly, there was a person in the grave reciting the surah of al-Mulk until he finished it. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'It is the preventer, it is the saviour; it saves him from the punishment of the grave.'"

After narrating it, al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a gharib hadith from this route."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "*Tabaraka* is the preventer from the punishment of the grave." It was also narrated by al-Nasa'i, who declared it sahih, and by al-Hakim.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Rafi' ibn Khadij and Abu Hurayrah that they both heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The surah of *Tabaraka* was revealed to me; it consists of thirty verses, all at once, and it is the preventer in the graves."

Abd ibn Humayd in his *Musnad*, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said to a man: "Shall I present you with a hadith that will make you happy?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Recite ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾, and teach it to your family, all your children, the children of your household, and your neighbours. For it is the saviour, and it is the advocate that will argue before its Lord on the Day of Resurrection on behalf of its reciter, and it will seek for him that Allah save him from the Fire, and its companion will be saved by it from the punishment of the grave."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I would love for it to be in the heart of every person in my Ummah."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His statement: ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾. *Tabaraka* is a form of *tafa'ala* from *barakah*, and *barakah* means growth and increase. It was also said: [it means] He is exalted and magnified above the attributes of created beings. It was also said: [it means] He endures; He is the Everlasting, whose existence has no beginning and whose permanence has no end.

Al-Hasan said: *Tabaraka* means "He is sanctified." The form *tafa'ala* is for emphasis (*mubalaghah*). The hand is a metaphor for power and control. *Al-mulk* is the dominion of the heavens and the earth in this world and the Hereafter; He honours whom He wills and humiliates whom He wills, He raises whom He wills and lowers whom He wills. It was also said: the intended meaning of *al-mulk* is the dominion of prophethood. The first [interpretation] is better, because interpreting it generally is more praiseworthy and more eloquent in praise, and there is no basis for specifying it.

﴿And He is Able over all things﴾: that is, He is perfectly capable; nothing among things can overpower Him. He disposes of His dominion however He wills, whether by bestowing favour or by retribution, by raising or lowering, by giving or withholding.

﴿He who created death and life﴾. Death is the cutting of the connection of the soul to the body and its separation from it; life is the connection of the soul to the body and its attachment to it. It was also said: life is that by whose existence perception becomes valid. It was also said: life is that which makes a thing alive. It was also said: the intended meaning is death in this world and life in the Hereafter.

Death is mentioned before life because the original state of things is the absence of life, and life is an accident attached to them. It was also said: because death is closer to subjugation.

Muqatil said: ﴿He created death﴾ means the sperm-drop, the lump of flesh, and the clot of blood; and ﴿life﴾ means that He created him as a human and created the soul in him. It was also said: He created death in the form of a ram, which does not pass by anything without killing it, and He created life in the form of a horse, which does not pass by anything without giving it life. This was said by Muqatil and al-Kalbi.

It has come in the revelation: ﴿Say: The angel of death who has been assigned to you will take you [in death]﴾ [Surah al-Sajdah: 11]; and His statement: ﴿If you could see when the angels take the disbelievers in death﴾ [Surah al-Anfal: 50]; and His statement: ﴿Our messengers take him in death﴾; and His statement: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [Surah al-Zumar: 42]; and other verses besides these.

It was also said: the meaning is: that He may test you, [to see] which of you remembers death most and is most fearful of it. It was also said: which of you is quickest to the obedience of Allah and most restrained from the prohibitions of Allah.

Al-Zajjaj said: the lam is connected to the creation of life, not to the creation of death.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' also said: His statement ﴿that He may test you﴾ does not govern ("fall upon") *ayyu* ("which"), because between the testing and *ayyu* there is an implied verb, as you say: "I tested you in order that I might see which of you is more obedient." ﴿The gaze will return to you humbled (*khasi'an*)﴾: that is, the gaze will return to you humiliated and abased, [unable] to see anything of that. It was also said: the meaning of *khasi'an*: distanced, expelled from seeing any defect it sought. It is said: "I drove away the dog" (*khasa'tu al-kalb*), meaning: I distanced and expelled it.

The majority read *yanqalib* ("will return") with *jazm* (apocopation) as an answer to the imperative. Al-Kisa'i, in one transmission, read it with *raf'* (nominative) as a new sentence.

﴿While it is fatigued (*hasir*)﴾: that is, weary, exhausted. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, it has become tired before it sees any flaw in the sky. *Hasir* is a form like *fa'il* in the meaning of *fa'il* (active), from *husur*, which is exhaustion. It is said: "His sight became *hasar*, *yahsur*, *husur*," meaning: it became weary and ceased. From it is the poet's saying:

*I looked at her in al-Muhassab of Mina, and the glance returned to me while it was fatigued.*

﴿And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps﴾. After creating the heavens and their being free of defect and flaw, Allah, glorified is He, explained that He adorned it with this adornment, so that it became in the best creation, the most perfect form, and the most delightful shape. The bringing of the oath is to show the completeness of care. *Al-masabih* is the plural of *misbah*, which is a lamp. The stars were named lamps because they shine like the shining of a lamp. Although some stars are in other heavens above it, they appear as though they are all in the nearest heaven, because the bodies of the heavens do not prevent seeing what is above them of things that give light, since they are polished, transparent bodies.

﴿And We have made them as missiles against the devils﴾: that is, and We made the lamps into projectiles with which the devils are stoned. This is a second benefit, other than the first, which is their being an adornment for the nearest heaven. The meaning is that the devils who eavesdrop are stoned with them. *Rujum* is the plural of *rajm*, with a *fatha*, and it is originally a verbal noun used for the thing with which one is stoned, as in their saying: "The dirham is the minting of the amir" (i.e., the minted thing). It may also remain as a verbal noun, and an omitted attributed noun is understood, meaning: possessors of stoning. The verbal noun is pluralized in consideration of its types.

It was also said: the pronoun in His statement "and We have made them" refers to the lamps with an omitted attributed noun, meaning: their meteors, which are their fire kindled from them, not the lamps themselves, due to His statement: ﴿Except one who snatches away a snatch, and is pursued by a piercing flame﴾ [Surah al-Saffat: 10]. The reasoning behind this is that the lamps with which Allah adorned the nearest heaven do not vanish and are not used for stoning. Abu Ali al-Farisi said this in answer to one who asked him: "How can the lamps be an adornment when they are projectiles?" Al-Qushayri said: "Better than this view is to say: they are an adornment before the devils are stoned with them."

Qatadah said: Allah created the stars for three purposes: as an adornment for the sky, as projectiles against the devils, and as signs by which one is guided on land and sea. Whoever speaks about them other than this has spoken about what he does not know, transgressed, and wronged [himself]. It was also said: the meaning of the verse is: We made them into conjectures for the devils of mankind, who are the astrologers.

﴿And We have prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze﴾: that is, and We have prepared for the devils, in the Hereafter, after burning in this world with the meteors, the punishment of the Blaze, that is, the punishment of the Fire. *Al-sa'ir* is the most intense burning; it is said: "The fire was kindled (*su''irat*), so it is *mas'urah*" (blazing).

﴿And for those who disbelieve in their Lord﴾: from among the disbelievers of the children of Adam, or from among the disbelievers of both groups (humans and jinn). ﴿is the punishment of Hell.﴾ The majority read *'adhab* ("punishment") with *raf'* (nominative), as the subject, and its predicate is *lilladhina kafaru* ("for those who disbelieve"). Al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, and al-A'raj read it with *nasb* (accusative), in coordination with ﴿the punishment of the Blaze﴾.

﴿And wretched is the destination.﴾ That is, the place to which they will return, namely Hell.

﴿When they are thrown into it﴾: that is, cast into it, as firewood is cast into the fire. ﴿they will hear from it a roaring (*shahiq*)﴾: that is, a sound like the braying of donkeys at the first start of their bray, and it is the most hideous of sounds. His statement "*laha*" ("from it") is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*): that is, [a roaring] existing from it. This is because originally it was an attribute, and when it was placed first, it became a circumstantial.

Ata said: "al-Shahiq" is the groaning of the disbelievers when they are thrown into the Fire. The clause ﴿wa-hiya tafur﴾ (﴿while it boils﴾) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while it is boiling with them, boiling like the cauldron (mirjal). From this is the saying of Hassan:

"You left your cooking pot with nothing in it, / while the pot of the caravan is hot and boiling."

﴿Takadu tamayyazu min al-ghayz﴾ means: it nearly splits apart, some of it separating from the rest out of its rage against them.

Ibn Qutaybah said: "It nearly bursts with fury against the disbelievers."

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "tamayyazu" with a single, lightened tā', while the original form is "tatamayyazu" with two tā's.

Ṭalḥah read it with two tā's, in the original form.

al-Bazzi, from Ibn Kathir, read it with a shadda, by assimilating one of the two tā's into the other.

al-Ḍaḥḥak read "tamāyaza" with an alif and a single tā', the original being "tatamāyazu." Zayd ibn ʿAli read "tamīza," from māza yamīzu. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, or in the nominative position as another predicate of a subject.

The clause ﴿kullama ulqiya fīha fawjun saʾalahum khazanatuha﴾ (﴿Whenever a group is thrown into it, its keepers ask them﴾) is a resumed clause explaining the state of its inhabitants, or it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "tamayyazu." The fawj is a group of people; meaning: whenever a group of disbelievers is thrown into Hell, its keepers, the angels, ask them a question of rebuke and reproach: ﴿Did there not come to you﴾ in the world ﴿a warner who warned you of this day and cautioned you against it?﴾

The clause ﴿qalu bala qad jaʾana nadhir﴾ (﴿They said: "Yes, indeed, a warner came to us"﴾) is a resumed clause answering an implied question, as if it had been said: "What did they say after this question?" So He said: ﴿They said: "Yes, indeed, a warner came to us, who warned us, frightened us, and informed us of this day, but we denied that warner."﴾ ﴿And we said: "Allah has not sent down anything"﴾ of things ﴿upon the tongues of you﴾ ﴿"You are only in great error"﴾, meaning: in going astray from the truth and distance from what is right.

The meaning is that each of those groups, relating to the keepers of Hell what had been said to them by those sent to them, says: "You, O messengers, in what you claim, that Allah has sent down to you signs by which you warn us, you are only in a great going astray from the truth and distance from what is right, which cannot be measured."

Then He related another saying of theirs, spoken after that saying: ﴿And they said: "Had we been listening or reasoning, we would not have been among the companions of the blaze."﴾ Meaning: had we listened to what the messengers addressed us with, or reasoned about any of it, we would not have been counted among the people of the Fire, or among those punished by the blaze, who are the devils, as has passed.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Had we listened with the hearing of one who comprehends, or reasoned with the reason of one who discerns and considers, we would not have been among the people of the Fire."

When they confessed this confession, Allah, glory be to Him, said: ﴿So they acknowledged their sin﴾, which made them deserving of the punishment of the Fire, namely disbelief and denial of the prophets. ﴿So away with the companions of the blaze﴾, meaning: far away from them, from Allah and from His mercy.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr and Abu Salih said: "It is a valley in Hell called al-Suḥq."

The majority read ﴿fasuḥqan﴾ with a sukun on the ḥā'. al-Kisai and Abu Jaʿfar read it with a ḍamma, and both are dialectal forms, like al-suḥt and al-ruʿb.

Al-Zajjaj and Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: "Fasuḥqan" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: Allah made them far away with a distancing.

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: "The analogical form would have been isḥāqan, but the verbal noun came with deletion." The lam in ﴿li-aṣḥab al-saʿir﴾ is for specification (bayān), as in ﴿hayta laka﴾ (Yusuf: 23).

ʿAbd ibn Humayd related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding ﴿seven heavens in layers (ṭibaqan)﴾, that he said: "some of them above others."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, regarding ﴿You will not see in the creation of the Most Merciful any inconsistency (tafawut)﴾, that he said: "Not one part of it differing from another in a dividing difference."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related also from him, regarding ﴿inconsistency (tafawut)﴾, that he said: "cracking (tashaqquq)." And regarding ﴿Do you see any rifts (futur)?﴾, he said: "cracks (shuquq)." And regarding ﴿despised (khasi'an)﴾, he said: "humiliated (dhalilan)," ﴿and he is fatigued (haseer)﴾: "weary (kalil)."

Ibn Jarir also related from him:
He said: "al-futur is al-wahy (cracking, fissure)."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him also, regarding ﴿rifts (futur)﴾: "cracking or flaw." And regarding ﴿the sight will return to you﴾: "it will return to you, ﴿despised (khasi'an)﴾: "humbled (saghiran)," ﴿and he is fatigued (haseer)﴾: "exhausted (ma'yiyy), seeing nothing."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him: ﴿despised (khasi'an)﴾: "humiliated (dhalilan)," ﴿and he is fatigued (haseer)﴾: "exhausted, turned back (muratja')."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿takadu tamayyazu﴾: "it nearly separates (tatafarraqu)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related also from him, ﴿takadu tamayyazu﴾: "some of it parts from others."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related also from him, ﴿fasuḥqan﴾: "distance (bu'dan)."

It is Meccan.
Al-Qurtubi said: "This is the consensus."

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The surah of *Tabaraka* (al-Mulk) was revealed in Mecca."

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Durays, al-Hakim (who declared it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, a surah from the Book of Allah, consisting of only thirty verses, interceded for a man until he was forgiven: ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾." Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a hasan hadith."

Al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat*, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtarah* narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A surah in the Qur'an argued on behalf of its companion until it brought him into Paradise: ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾."

Al-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim (who declared it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, Ibn Nasr, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated from Ibn (p-1510) Abbas, who said: "One of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) pitched his tent over a grave, while he did not realize it was a grave. Suddenly, there was a person in the grave reciting the surah of al-Mulk until he finished it. He came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'It is the preventer, it is the saviour; it saves him from the punishment of the grave.'"

After narrating it, al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a gharib hadith from this route."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "*Tabaraka* is the preventer from the punishment of the grave." It was also narrated by al-Nasa'i, who declared it sahih, and by al-Hakim.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Rafi' ibn Khadij and Abu Hurayrah that they both heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The surah of *Tabaraka* was revealed to me; it consists of thirty verses, all at once, and it is the preventer in the graves."

Abd ibn Humayd in his *Musnad*, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said to a man: "Shall I present you with a hadith that will make you happy?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Recite ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾, and teach it to your family, all your children, the children of your household, and your neighbours. For it is the saviour, and it is the advocate that will argue before its Lord on the Day of Resurrection on behalf of its reciter, and it will seek for him that Allah save him from the Fire, and its companion will be saved by it from the punishment of the grave."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I would love for it to be in the heart of every person in my Ummah."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His statement: ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion﴾. *Tabaraka* is a form of *tafa'ala* from *barakah*, and *barakah* means growth and increase. It was also said: [it means] He is exalted and magnified above the attributes of created beings. It was also said: [it means] He endures; He is the Everlasting, whose existence has no beginning and whose permanence has no end.

Al-Hasan said: *Tabaraka* means "He is sanctified." The form *tafa'ala* is for emphasis (*mubalaghah*). The hand is a metaphor for power and control. *Al-mulk* is the dominion of the heavens and the earth in this world and the Hereafter; He honours whom He wills and humiliates whom He wills, He raises whom He wills and lowers whom He wills. It was also said: the intended meaning of *al-mulk* is the dominion of prophethood. The first [interpretation] is better, because interpreting it generally is more praiseworthy and more eloquent in praise, and there is no basis for specifying it.

﴿And He is Able over all things﴾: that is, He is perfectly capable; nothing among things can overpower Him. He disposes of His dominion however He wills, whether by bestowing favour or by retribution, by raising or lowering, by giving or withholding.

﴿He who created death and life﴾. Death is the cutting of the connection of the soul to the body and its separation from it; life is the connection of the soul to the body and its attachment to it. It was also said: life is that by whose existence perception becomes valid. It was also said: life is that which makes a thing alive. It was also said: the intended meaning is death in this world and life in the Hereafter.

Death is mentioned before life because the original state of things is the absence of life, and life is an accident attached to them. It was also said: because death is closer to subjugation.

Muqatil said: ﴿He created death﴾ means the sperm-drop, the lump of flesh, and the clot of blood; and ﴿life﴾ means that He created him as a human and created the soul in him. It was also said: He created death in the form of a ram, which does not pass by anything without killing it, and He created life in the form of a horse, which does not pass by anything without giving it life. This was said by Muqatil and al-Kalbi.

It has come in the revelation: ﴿Say: The angel of death who has been assigned to you will take you [in death]﴾ [Surah al-Sajdah: 11]; and His statement: ﴿If you could see when the angels take the disbelievers in death﴾ [Surah al-Anfal: 50]; and His statement: ﴿Our messengers take him in death﴾; and His statement: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾ [Surah al-Zumar: 42]; and other verses besides these.

﴿That He may test you [to see] which of you is best in deed﴾: The lam is connected to *khalaqa* ("created"); that is, He created death and life in order to deal with you as one who tests you, [to see] which of you is best in deed, and then He will recompense you for that. It was also said: the meaning is: that He may test you, [to see] which of you remembers death most and is most fearful of it. It was also said: which of you is quickest to the obedience of Allah and most restrained from the prohibitions of Allah.

Al-Zajjaj said: the lam is connected to the creation of life, not to the creation of death.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' also said: His statement ﴿that He may test you﴾ does not govern ("fall upon") *ayyu* ("which"), because between the testing and *ayyu* there is an implied verb, as you say: "I tested you in order that I might see which of you is more obedient." Its like is His statement: ﴿Ask them which of them will vouch for that﴾ [Surah al-Qalam: 40], meaning: ask them, then look at which of them [will]. Thus *ayyukum* ("which of you") in the verse is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is *ahsan* ("best"), because an interrogative does not allow what precedes it to govern it.

The use of the comparative form, although the testing encompasses all their actions, which are divided into good and bad and not merely into good and better, is to announce that the primary and essential purpose of testing is the manifestation of the perfection of the goodness of the good-doers.

﴿He is the Mighty (al-'Aziz), i.e., the Overpowering who cannot be overpowered, the Forgiving (al-Ghafur) to whoever repents and turns back.﴾

﴿He who created seven heavens in layers﴾. The relative pronoun (*al-ladhi*) may be a follower of *al-'Aziz al-Ghafur*, either as an adjective (*na't*), as an explanatory apposition (*bayan*), or as a substitute (*badal*). It may also be disconnected from it, being the predicate of an omitted subject, or in the accusative as a praise (*mad*). *Tibaqan* ("in layers") is an attributive of "seven heavens", meaning: some of them above others. It is the plural of *tabaq* like *jabal* / *jibal* ("mountain / mountains"), or the plural of *tabaqah* like *rahbah* / *rihab* ("courtyard / courtyards"), or a verbal noun of *taabaqa*. It is said: *taabaqa*, *mutabaqah* and *tibaqan*. On this last view the attribute is a verbal noun for emphasis, or [the phrase is] with an omitted attributed noun, meaning: possessing layers. It may also be in the accusative as a verbal noun with an omitted verb, meaning: they were made into layers (*tubiqat tibaqan*).

﴿You will not see in the creation of the Most Gracious any discrepancy.﴾ This sentence is a second attribute of "seven heavens", or is a new sentence confirming what precedes it. The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone who is suitable for it. *Min* is additional, for emphasis of the negation.

The majority read ﴿min tafawut﴾ ("any discrepancy"). Ibn Mas'ud and his companions, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read *tafawut* (with *tashdid*, without an *alif*) — *tafawwut*. Both are two dialects, like *al-ta'ahhud* and *al-ta'hhud*, and *al-tahammul* and *al-tahammul*. The meaning according to both readings is: you will not see in the creation of the Most Gracious any contradiction, any disparity, any crookedness, or any inconsistency; rather, it is uniform, straight, and indicative of its Creator. Even though their forms and attributes differ, they agree in this respect.

﴿So return the gaze; do you see any rifts?﴾ *Futur* means cracks, fissures, and holes. That is: return your glance until that becomes clear to you by direct observation.

First He informed that there is no discrepancy in His creation; then He commanded, a second time, the repeated looking at that, for increased confirmation and the attainment of tranquillity.

Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: *al-futur* means cracks; it is the plural of *fatr*, which is a split.

Qatadah said: "Do you see any flaw?"

Al-Suddi said: "Do you see any holes?" Its root is from *tafattur* and *infitar*, which is splitting and cleaving. From it is the poet's saying:

*He built for you a sky without pillars, and adorned it, and there is no fissure in it.*

And the saying of another:

*You split the heart, then you returned to it your love, [so] the wound healed and the fissures closed up.*

﴿Then return the gaze twice﴾: that is, two returns, one time after another. Its accusative is as a verbal noun. The meaning of the dual is multiplication, as in *labbayka* and *sa'dayka* ("at Your service, again and again"). That is: a return after a return, however many times.

The rationale for commanding the repetition of looking in this manner is that one may not see the defect one thinks there is at the first glance, nor at the second.

For this reason He said first ﴿You will not see in the creation of the Most Gracious any discrepancy﴾, then said secondly ﴿So return the gaze﴾, then said thirdly ﴿Then return the gaze twice﴾. This is more eloquent in establishing the proof and more decisive in cutting off excuses.

﴿The gaze will return to you humbled (*khasi'an*)﴾: that is, the gaze will return to you humiliated and abased, [unable] to see anything of that. It was also said: the meaning of *khasi'an*: distanced, expelled from seeing any defect it sought. It is said: "I drove away the dog" (*khasa'tu al-kalb*), meaning: I distanced and expelled it.

The majority read *yanqalib* ("will return") with *jazm* (apocopation) as an answer to the imperative. Al-Kisa'i, in one transmission, read it with *raf'* (nominative) as a new sentence.

﴿While it is fatigued (*hasir*)﴾: that is, weary, exhausted. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, it has become tired before it sees any flaw in the sky. *Hasir* is a form like *fa'il* in the meaning of *fa'il* (active), from *husur*, which is exhaustion. It is said: "His sight became *hasar*, *yahsur*, *husur*," meaning: it became weary and ceased. From it is the poet's saying:

*I looked at her in al-Muhassab of Mina, and the glance returned to me while it was fatigued.*

﴿And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps﴾. After creating the heavens and their being free of defect and flaw, Allah, glorified is He, explained that He adorned it with this adornment, so that it became in the best creation, the most perfect form, and the most delightful shape. The bringing of the oath is to show the completeness of care. *Al-masabih* is the plural of *misbah*, which is a lamp. The stars were named lamps because they shine like the shining of a lamp. Although some stars are in other heavens above it, they appear as though they are all in the nearest heaven, because the bodies of the heavens do not prevent seeing what is above them of things that give light, since they are polished, transparent bodies.

﴿And We have made them as missiles against the devils﴾: that is, and We made the lamps into projectiles with which the devils are stoned. The meaning is that the devils who eavesdrop are stoned with them. *Rujum* is the plural of *rajm*, with a *fatha*, and it is originally a verbal noun used for the thing with which one is stoned, as in their saying: "The dirham is the minting of the amir" (i.e., the minted thing). It may also remain as a verbal noun, and an omitted attributed noun is understood, meaning: possessors of stoning. The verbal noun is pluralized in consideration of its types.

It was also said: the pronoun in His statement "and We have made them" refers to the lamps with an omitted attributed noun, meaning: their meteors, which are their fire kindled from them, not the lamps themselves, due to His statement: ﴿Except one who snatches away a snatch, and is pursued by a piercing flame﴾ [Surah al-Saffat: 10]. The reasoning behind this is that the lamps with which Allah adorned the nearest heaven do not vanish and are not used for stoning. Abu Ali al-Farisi said this in answer to one who asked him: "How can the lamps be an adornment when they are projectiles?" Al-Qushayri said: "Better than this view is to say: they are an adornment before the devils are stoned with them."

Qatadah said: Allah created the stars for three purposes: as an adornment for the sky, as projectiles against the devils, and as signs by which one is guided on land and sea. Whoever speaks about them other than this has spoken about what he does not know, transgressed, and wronged [himself]. It was also said: the meaning of the verse is: We made them into conjectures for the devils of mankind, who are the astrologers.

﴿And We have prepared for them the punishment of the Blaze﴾: that is, and We have prepared for the devils, in the Hereafter, after burning in this world with the meteors, the punishment of the Blaze, that is, the punishment of the Fire. *Al-sa'ir* is the most intense burning; it is said: "The fire was kindled (*su''irat*), so it is *mas'urah*" (blazing).

﴿And for those who disbelieve in their Lord﴾: from among the disbelievers of the children of Adam, or from among the disbelievers of both groups (humans and jinn). ﴿is the punishment of Hell.﴾ The majority read *'adhab* ("punishment") with *raf'* (nominative), as the subject, and its predicate is *lilladhina kafaru* ("for those who disbelieve"). Al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, and al-A'raj read it with *nasb* (accusative), in coordination with ﴿the punishment of the Blaze﴾.

﴿And wretched is the destination.﴾ That is, the place to which they will return, namely Hell.

﴿When they are thrown into it﴾: that is, cast into it, as firewood is cast into the fire. ﴿they will hear from it a roaring (*shahiq*)﴾: that is, a sound like the braying of donkeys at the first start of their bray, and it is the most hideous of sounds. His statement "*laha*" ("from it") is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial (*hal*): that is, [a roaring] existing from it. This is because originally it was an attribute, and when it was placed first, it became a circumstantial.

Ata said: "al-Shahiq" is the groaning of the disbelievers when they are thrown into the Fire. The clause ﴿wa-hiya tafur﴾ (﴿while it boils﴾) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while it is boiling with them, boiling like the cauldron (mirjal). From this is the saying of Hassan:

"You left your cooking pot with nothing in it, / while the pot of the caravan is hot and boiling."

Ibn Qutaybah said: "It nearly bursts with fury against the disbelievers."
