Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 67, verse 12–21:

His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who fear their Lord unseen, for them is forgiveness and a great reward.﴾ When He, glorified is He, finished mentioning the states of the people of the Fire, He mentioned the people of Paradise. "Unseen" (bil-ghayb) is a circumstantial phrase (hal) either from the subject or from the object, meaning: being absent from Him, or Him being absent from them. The meaning is that they fear His punishment without having seen it, and so they believe in Him out of fear of His punishment. It is also possible that the meaning is: they fear their Lord while being absent from people's eyes, and that is in their private moments. Or the intended meaning of "unseen" is that the punishment is absent from them because they are in this world, and it only occurs on the Day of Resurrection; in this case the bā' is causal. ﴿For them is forgiveness﴾, a great one by which Allah forgives their sins, ﴿and a great reward﴾, which is Paradise. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿Whoever feared the Most Merciful unseen﴾ [Qaf: 33].

Then He, glorified is He, returned to addressing the disbelievers, saying: ﴿And keep your speech secret or speak it openly, indeed He is Knower of what is within the breasts.﴾ This sentence is a resumptive one, brought to explain the equality of secrecy and openness with respect to the knowledge of Allah, glorified is He. The meaning: whether you conceal your speech or declare it openly concerning the matter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), all of it Allah knows; nothing from it is hidden from Him. The clause ﴿Indeed He is Knower of what is within the breasts﴾ is a justification (ta'līl) for the equality mentioned. Dhāt al-ṣudūr ("what is within the breasts") is the concealed contents of the hearts.

The interrogative in His saying: ﴿Should not He who created know?﴾ is for denial. The meaning: Should not He know the secret, and the concealed contents of the hearts? He who created that and brought it into being. So the relative pronoun refers to the Creator. It is also possible that it refers to the created, and in "yaʿlamu" there is a pronoun referring to Allah; that is: should not Allah know the created being which is among His creation, for secrecy, openness and the concealed contents of the hearts are among His creation. The clause ﴿And He is the Subtle, the Acquainted﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "yaʿlamu", meaning the One whose knowledge of what is in the hearts is subtle, the Acquainted with what you conceal and hide of matters; nothing of that is hidden from Him.

Then He, glorified is He, bestowed favour upon His servants, saying: ﴿It is He who made the earth docile for you﴾, meaning: easy and soft, upon which you settle; He did not make it rough such that sitting upon it and walking on it would be impossible for you. The word dhalūl (docile) originally means the one that is submissive, which yields to you and is not difficult for you; its verbal noun is al-dhull. The fā' in His saying: ﴿So walk in its shoulders﴾ indicates the ordering of the command to walk upon the making mentioned, and the command is for permission.

Mujāhid, al-Kalbī and Muqātil said: its "manākib" are its paths, its sides and its edges.

Qatādah and Shahr ibn Ḥawshab said: its "manākib" are its mountains. The origin of mankib is the side, and from it comes "mankib al-rajul" (the shoulder of a man), and from it the "nakbāʾ" wind, because it comes from one side and not another. ﴿And eat of His provision﴾, meaning: of what He has provided and created for you on the earth. ﴿And to Him is the resurrection﴾, meaning: to Him is the raising from your graves, not to other than Him; and in this is a severe warning. (p-1513)

Then He, glorified is He, instilled fear in the disbelievers.

He said: ﴿Are you secure from He who is in the heaven that He will cause the earth to swallow you?﴾ Al-Wāḥidī said: the exegetes said, meaning: the punishment of He who is in the heaven. It was said: "He who is in the heaven" is His power, His authority, His throne and His angels. It was said: "He who is in the heaven" refers to the angels. It was said: the intended one is Jibrīl. The meaning of ﴿that He will cause the earth to swallow you﴾ is that He uproots it with you in it, as He did with Qārūn, after He had made it docile for you so that you walk in its shoulders. His saying: ﴿that He will cause to swallow﴾ is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) from the relative pronoun, meaning: are you secure from His causing you to be swallowed; or it is with the omission of "min", meaning: from that He will cause to swallow. ﴿Then behold, it shakes﴾, meaning: it quivers and moves contrary to the stillness it had been in.

The majority read "a-amintum" with two hamzas; the Basrans and Kufans read with lightening, and Ibn Kathīr read by changing the first into a wāw.

Then He, glorified is He, repeated the threat to them in another way, saying: ﴿Or are you secure from He who is in the heaven that He will send upon you a sandstorm?﴾ meaning: stones from the sky, as He sent them upon the people of Lot and the companions of the Elephant. It was said: a cloud in which are stones; it was said: a wind in which are stones. ﴿Then you will know how My warning was﴾, meaning: My warning when you witness the punishment, and this knowledge will not benefit you. It was said: the "nadhīr" here is Muhammad (ﷺ), as said by ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

The meaning: you will know My messenger and his truthfulness. The first is preferred.

The discussion of ﴿that He will send upon you a sandstorm﴾ is like the discussion of ﴿that He will cause the earth to swallow you﴾; so it is either a substitution of inclusion, or with the estimate of "min".

﴿And those before them certainly denied﴾, meaning those before the disbelievers of Makkah, from the disbelieving past nations.

Such as the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd, the people of Lot, the companions of the Thicket (al-Aykah), the companions of the Rass, and the people of Pharaoh. ﴿So how was My disapproval?﴾, meaning: how was My rejection of them, with what I afflicted them with of terrible punishment.

﴿Have they not considered the birds above them, spreading their wings and folding them?﴾ The hamza is for interrogation and the wāw for conjunction upon an implied clause, meaning: have they been heedless and not looked? The meaning of ṣāffāt is that they spread their wings in the air and extend them when flying. ﴿And folding﴾, meaning: they gather their wings.

Al-Naḥḥās said: it is said of a bird when it spreads its wing that it is ṣāff, and when it folds it, that it is qābiḍ, as if it is gripping it; and this is the meaning of flying, which is spreading the wing and then folding it after spreading. From it is the saying of Abū Khirāsh:

"He hastens the wing of night, so it departs, under the wing with spreading and folding."

He said "wa-yaqbiḍna" and did not say "qābiḍāt" as he said "ṣāffāt", because folding recurs from time to time, while spreading is the basic state. Thus it has been said.

It was also said that the meaning of "wa-yaqbiḍna" is their folding of their wings when they halt from flying, not their folding while in flight. The clause ﴿None holds them up except the Most Merciful﴾ is in an accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "yaqbiḍna", or it is a resumed sentence to explain the perfection of Allah's power, glorified is He. The meaning: none holds them in the air during flight except the Most Merciful, the One who is capable of everything. ﴿Indeed He is, of everything, Seeing﴾, nothing is hidden from Him, whatever it may be.

﴿Who is this that is an army for you to support you other than the Most Merciful?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach. The meaning: there is no army for you to prevent you from the punishment of Allah. The word "jund" means a party and a defence.

The majority read "amman hādhā" with a shaddah on the mīm, by assimilating the mīm of "am" into the mīm of "man"; and "am" here means "bal" (rather). There is no way to estimate a hamza after it as is usual in estimating the disjunctive "am" as "bal" plus hamza, because after it here is the interrogative "man", which suffices in place of that estimate. The interrogative "man" is a subject (mubtada'), and the demonstrative is its predicate; the relative pronoun with its clause is an attribute of the demonstrative; "yanṣurukum" is an attribute of "jund"; and "min dūni al-Raḥmān" is in an accusative position as a circumstantial phrase from the subject of "yanṣurukum". The meaning: rather, who is this contemptible one who, in your assumption, is an army for you, going beyond the support of the Most Merciful? Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif read with lightening the first and emphasis on the second. The clause ﴿The disbelievers are only in delusion﴾ is a parenthetical sentence confirming what came before and condemning them for the error they are in. The meaning: the disbelievers are only in great delusion from the side of Satan, who deceives them with it.

Such as the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd, the people of Lot, the companions of the Thicket (al-Aykah), the companions of the Rass, and the people of Pharaoh. ﴿So how was My disapproval?﴾, meaning: how was My rejection of them, with what I afflicted them with of terrible punishment.

﴿Have they not considered the birds above them, spreading their wings and folding them?﴾ The hamza is for interrogation and the wāw for conjunction upon an implied clause, meaning: have they been heedless and not looked? The meaning of ṣāffāt is that they spread their wings in the air and extend them when flying. ﴿And folding﴾, meaning: they gather their wings.

Al-Naḥḥās said: it is said of a bird when it spreads its wing that it is ṣāff, and when it folds it, that it is qābiḍ, as if it is gripping it; and this is the meaning of flying, which is spreading the wing and then folding it after spreading. From it is the saying of Abū Khirāsh:

"He hastens the wing of night, so it departs, under the wing with spreading and folding."

He said "wa-yaqbiḍna" and did not say "qābiḍāt" as he said "ṣāffāt", because folding recurs from time to time, while spreading is the basic state. Thus it has been said.

It was also said that the meaning of "wa-yaqbiḍna" is their folding of their wings when they halt from flying, not their folding while in flight. The clause ﴿None holds them up except the Most Merciful﴾ is in an accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "yaqbiḍna", or it is a resumed sentence to explain the perfection of Allah's power, glorified is He. The meaning: none holds them in the air during flight except the Most Merciful, the One who is capable of everything. ﴿Indeed He is, of everything, Seeing﴾, nothing is hidden from Him, whatever it may be.

﴿Who is this that is an army for you to support you other than the Most Merciful?﴾ The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach. The meaning: there is no army for you to prevent you from the punishment of Allah. The word "jund" means a party and a defence.

The majority read "amman hādhā" with a shaddah on the mīm, by assimilating the mīm of "am" into the mīm of "man"; and "am" here means "bal" (rather). There is no way to estimate a hamza after it as is usual in estimating the disjunctive "am" as "bal" plus hamza, because after it here is the interrogative "man", which suffices in place of that estimate. The interrogative "man" is a subject (mubtada'), and the demonstrative is its predicate; the relative pronoun with its clause is an attribute of the demonstrative; "yanṣurukum" is an attribute of "jund"; and "min dūni al-Raḥmān" is in an accusative position as a circumstantial phrase from the subject of "yanṣurukum". The meaning: rather, who is this contemptible one who, in your assumption, is an army for you, going beyond the support of the Most Merciful? Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif read with lightening the first and emphasis on the second. The clause ﴿The disbelievers are only in delusion﴾ is a parenthetical sentence confirming what came before and condemning them for the error they are in. The meaning: the disbelievers are only in great delusion from the side of Satan, who deceives them with it.

﴿Who is this that provides for you if He withholds His provision?﴾ The discussion of this is like the discussion of the previous one in recitation and grammar, meaning: who is it that pours down provision upon you from rain and other things, if Allah withholds that from you and prevents it from you? ﴿Rather they persist in insolence and aversion﴾, meaning: they were not affected by that; rather they persisted in obstinacy and arrogance against the truth and aversion from it, and they did not take heed nor reflect. The answer to the condition is omitted, indicated by what precedes it: if He withholds His provision, then who else will provide for you? The word ʿutuw means obstinacy and transgression, and nufūr means fleeing.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿Indeed, those who fear their Lord unseen﴾ that he said: they are Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿAlī, and Abū ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrāḥ.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him regarding ﴿in its shoulders﴾ that he said: its mountains.

Ibn Jarīr also transmitted from him that he said: its edges.

al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn ʿAdī, al-Bayhaqī in al-Shuʿab, and al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī transmitted from Ibn ʿUmar who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah loves the believing servant who practises a trade."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿Rather they persist in insolence and aversion﴾ that he said: in misguidance.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who fear their Lord unseen, for them is forgiveness and a great reward.﴾ When He, glorified is He, finished mentioning the states of the people of the Fire, He mentioned the people of Paradise. "Unseen" (bil-ghayb) is a circumstantial phrase (hal) either from the subject or from the object, meaning: being absent from Him, or Him being absent from them. The meaning is that they fear His punishment without having seen it, and so they believe in Him out of fear of His punishment. It is also possible that the meaning is: they fear their Lord while being absent from people's eyes, and that is in their private moments. Or the intended meaning of "unseen" is that the punishment is absent from them because they are in this world, and it only occurs on the Day of Resurrection; in this case the bā' is causal. ﴿For them is forgiveness﴾, a great one by which Allah forgives their sins, ﴿and a great reward﴾, which is Paradise. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿Whoever feared the Most Merciful unseen﴾ [Qaf: 33].

Then He, glorified is He, returned to addressing the disbelievers, saying: ﴿And keep your speech secret or speak it openly, indeed He is Knower of what is within the breasts.﴾ This sentence is a resumptive one, brought to explain the equality of secrecy and openness with respect to the knowledge of Allah, glorified is He. The meaning: whether you conceal your speech or declare it openly concerning the matter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), all of it Allah knows; nothing from it is hidden from Him. The clause ﴿Indeed He is Knower of what is within the breasts﴾ is a justification (ta'līl) for the equality mentioned. Dhāt al-ṣudūr ("what is within the breasts") is the concealed contents of the hearts.

The interrogative in His saying: ﴿Should not He who created know?﴾ is for denial. The meaning: Should not He know the secret, and the concealed contents of the hearts? He who created that and brought it into being. So the relative pronoun refers to the Creator. It is also possible that it refers to the created, and in "yaʿlamu" there is a pronoun referring to Allah; that is: should not Allah know the created being which is among His creation, for secrecy, openness and the concealed contents of the hearts are among His creation. The clause ﴿And He is the Subtle, the Acquainted﴾ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "yaʿlamu", meaning the One whose knowledge of what is in the hearts is subtle, the Acquainted with what you conceal and hide of matters; nothing of that is hidden from Him.

Then He, glorified is He, bestowed favour upon His servants, saying: ﴿It is He who made the earth docile for you﴾, meaning: easy and soft, upon which you settle; He did not make it rough such that sitting upon it and walking on it would be impossible for you. The word dhalūl (docile) originally means the one that is submissive, which yields to you and is not difficult for you; its verbal noun is al-dhull. The fā' in His saying: ﴿So walk in its shoulders﴾ indicates the ordering of the command to walk upon the making mentioned, and the command is for permission.

Mujāhid, al-Kalbī and Muqātil said: its "manākib" are its paths, its sides and its edges.

Qatādah and Shahr ibn Ḥawshab said: its "manākib" are its mountains. The origin of mankib is the side, and from it comes "mankib al-rajul" (the shoulder of a man), and from it the "nakbāʾ" wind, because it comes from one side and not another. ﴿And eat of His provision﴾, meaning: of what He has provided and created for you on the earth. ﴿And to Him is the resurrection﴾, meaning: to Him is the raising from your graves, not to other than Him; and in this is a severe warning. (p-1513)

Then He, glorified is He, instilled fear in the disbelievers.

He said: ﴿Are you secure from He who is in the heaven that He will cause the earth to swallow you?﴾ Al-Wāḥidī said: the exegetes said, meaning: the punishment of He who is in the heaven. It was said: "He who is in the heaven" is His power, His authority, His throne and His angels. It was said: "He who is in the heaven" refers to the angels. It was said: the intended one is Jibrīl. The meaning of ﴿that He will cause the earth to swallow you﴾ is that He uproots it with you in it, as He did with Qārūn, after He had made it docile for you so that you walk in its shoulders. His saying: ﴿that He will cause to swallow﴾ is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) from the relative pronoun, meaning: are you secure from His causing you to be swallowed; or it is with the omission of "min", meaning: from that He will cause to swallow. ﴿Then behold, it shakes﴾, meaning: it quivers and moves contrary to the stillness it had been in.

The majority read "a-amintum" with two hamzas; the Basrans and Kufans read with lightening, and Ibn Kathīr read by changing the first into a wāw.

Then He, glorified is He, repeated the threat to them in another way, saying: ﴿Or are you secure from He who is in the heaven that He will send upon you a sandstorm?﴾ meaning: stones from the sky, as He sent them upon the people of Lot and the companions of the Elephant. It was said: a cloud in which are stones; it was said: a wind in which are stones. ﴿Then you will know how My warning was﴾, meaning: My warning when you witness the punishment, and this knowledge will not benefit you. It was said: the "nadhīr" here is Muhammad (ﷺ), as said by ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

The meaning: you will know My messenger and his truthfulness. The first is preferred.

The discussion of ﴿that He will send upon you a sandstorm﴾ is like the discussion of ﴿that He will cause the earth to swallow you﴾; so it is either a substitution of inclusion, or with the estimate of "min".

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 67, verses 22–30:

Allah, glory be to Him, struck an example of the polytheist and the monotheist to clarify their condition and explain their final outcome. He said: ﴿Is one who walks prostrate on his face better guided, or one who walks upright on a straight path?﴾ Al-mukibb and al-munkabb are the one who falls on his face. It is said: "I made him fall (kababtuhu), so he fell (akabba and inkabba)." It was also said: he is the one who bows his head and does not look right, left, or ahead, so he is never safe from stumbling and falling on his face.

It was also said: he means the blind man who does not find the way, so his walking continually makes him fall on his face.

Qatadah said: He is the disbeliever who falls into the disobedience of Allah in this world, so Allah will gather him on the Day of Resurrection on his face.

The hamzah is an interrogative of denial, meaning: Is this one who walks on his face better guided to the goal he seeks, or the one who walks upright, ﴿upright﴾, balanced, looking at what is before him, ﴿on a straight path﴾, meaning on a level road with no crookedness or deviation in it? The predicate of "man" (the second) is omitted, because the predicate of the first "man", which is "better guided", indicates it. It was said: there is no need for that, because the second "man" is conjoined to the first "man" by a conjunction of singular to singular, like your saying: "Is Zayd standing, or 'Amr?" It was said: by "one who walks prostrate on his face" he means one who will be gathered on his face to the Fire, and by "one who walks upright" he means one who will be gathered on his feet to Paradise. This is like the statement of Qatadah that we mentioned, and similar to it is His saying: ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces﴾ [al-Isra: 97].

﴿Say: He it is who brought you into being⟩ Allah, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger ﷺ to inform them that Allah is the One who brought them into existence in the first creation, and made for them hearing so that they might hear with it, and sight so that they might see with it. The reason the word "hearing" is singular while "sights" is plural is that it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) which applies to the few and the many. We have already explained this in several places, with additional clarification. And the hearts (al-af'idah) are the hearts with which they reflect upon the creatures of Allah. So He, glory be to Him, mentions here that He has given them what they perceive heard things, seen things and intelligible things, as a clarification of the proof, a cutting off of excuse, and a rebuke for them for not being thankful for the blessings of Allah. Therefore He said: ﴿Little is it that you give thanks.﴾ The accusative of "qalilan" is because it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, and "ma" is added for emphasis, meaning: a little thanks, or for a little time. It was also said: by the paucity of thanks he means its non-existence among them.

Muqatil said: He means that you do not thank the Lord of these blessings so that you would affirm His oneness.

﴿Say: He it is who multiplied you upon the earth, and to Him you will be gathered.﴾ Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ to inform them that Allah is the One who created them on the earth, spread them out in it, and dispersed them over its surface, and that their gathering for recompense is to Him, not to anyone else.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned that they seek to hasten the punishment, so He said: ﴿And they say: When is this promise, if you are truthful?⟩ meaning: when is this promise that you mention to us, of the gathering, the Resurrection, the Fire and the punishment, if you are truthful in that?

The address from them is to the Prophet ﷺ and to those with him among the believers. The response to the condition is omitted, and the implied meaning is: if you are truthful, then inform us of it, or then explain it to us.

This from them is mockery and derision.

Then, when they said this statement, Allah, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger ﷺ to respond to them, so He said: ﴿Say: Knowledge is only with Allah⟩, meaning: the knowledge of the time of the Hour is with Allah alone, and no one else knows it.

Similar to it is His saying: ﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 187]. Then He informed them that he was sent only as a warner, not to inform them of the unseen, so He said: ﴿And I am only a clear warner⟩, I warn you and make you fear the consequence of your disbelief, and I make clear to you what Allah has commanded me to make clear.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned their condition at the sight of the punishment, so He said: ﴿But when they see it close⟩, meaning: they see the punishment as near. "Zulfah" is a verbal noun in the sense of the active participle, meaning: approaching; or it is a circumstantial accusative from the object of "they see", with an elided modifier, meaning: possessing nearness and closeness.

Or it is an adverb of place, meaning: they see it in a place that is near.

Mujahid said: that is, near.

Al-Hasan said: face to face.

Most exegetes said: what is meant is the punishment of the Day of Resurrection. Mujahid said: what is meant is the punishment of Badr. It was also said: they saw what they were promised of the gathering close to them, as His saying indicates: ﴿and to Him you will be gathered.⟩ It was also said: when they see their evil deeds close, ﴿the faces of those who disbelieved will be made evil⟩, meaning they will turn black, covered with dejection and overcome with humiliation. It is said: "sa'a al-shay'u yasu'u fa-huwa sayyi'" when a thing becomes ugly.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that evil becomes manifest in them, i.e., that punishment distresses them, and because of it there appears on their faces what shows their disbelief, like His saying: ﴿On the Day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black﴾ [Al 'Imran: 106].

The majority read "sī'at" with a kasrah on the sin without ishmam. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Muhaysin read it with ishmam. ﴿And it will be said: This is what you used to call for⟩, meaning: it is said to them as reproach and rebuke: this visible, present punishment is the punishment that you used to call for in the world, meaning you were seeking it and hastening it in mockery, on the basis that the meaning of "tad'un" is "du'a" (calling/supplicating).

Al-Farra' said: "tadda'una" is from "du'a", meaning: you wish for it and ask for it, and most exegetes said this.

Al-Zajjaj said: "This is what you used to claim" refers to the falsehoods and tales.

It was also said: the meaning of "tadda'un" is "you lie." This is on the recitation of the majority, "tadda'un" with shaddah, so it is either from "du'a" as most said, or from "da'wa" (claim) as al-Zajjaj and those who agreed with him said, and the meaning is: they used to claim that there is no resurrection, no gathering, no Paradise and no Fire.

Qatadah and Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ya'qub and al-Dahhak read "tad'un" without shaddah, and its meaning is clear.

Qatadah said: it is their saying: ﴿Our Lord, hasten for us our portion﴾ [Sad: 16]. Al-Dahhak said: it is their saying: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], the verse.

Al-Nahhas said: "tadda'un" and "tad'un" have one meaning, as you say "qadara" and "iqtadara", and "ghada" and "ightada", except that "af'ala" means it passed one thing after another, while "fi'l" applies to the few and the many.

﴿Say: Have you considered, if Allah destroys me and those with me⟩, meaning: inform me, if Allah destroys me and those with me by punishment, or has mercy on us and does not punish us, ﴿then who will protect the disbelievers from a painful punishment?⟩, meaning: who will protect them and secure them from the punishment.

The meaning is: none will save them from that, whether Allah destroys His Messenger and the believers with him, as the disbelievers were wishing, or grants them respite.

It was also said: the meaning is: we, with our faith, are between fear and hope, so who will protect you, with your disbelief, from the punishment? The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun in order to brand them with disbelief and to show that it is the cause of their not being saved.

﴿Say: He is the Most Merciful; we have believed in Him⟩ alone, we associate nothing with Him, ﴿and upon Him we have relied⟩ and not upon anyone else.

Tawakkul is committing affairs to Him, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿So you will know who is in clear error⟩, we or you.

In this is a severe threat, with the speech presented in the manner of fairness.

The majority read "sata'lamun" with the second person (ta). Al-Kisa'i read it with the third person (ya), as a report.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, argued against them with some of His blessings, and made them fear the removal of that blessing from them, so He said: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should become sunken⟩, meaning: inform me, if your water becomes absorbed into the earth so that no trace of it remains in it at all, or it goes away into the earth to a far place so that buckets cannot reach it.

It is said: "ghaara al-ma'u ghawran," meaning it receded. "Al-ghawr" is the sunken, described by a verbal noun for emphasis, as one says "rajul 'adl" (a just man). A similar case has already been mentioned in Surat al-Kahf. ﴿Then who will bring you clear water?⟩, meaning apparent water that eyes can see and buckets can reach. It was also said: it is from "ma'ana al-ma'u", meaning it became abundant.

Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: it means flowing. The meaning of "ma'in" has already been mentioned in Surat al-Mu'min.

Ibn 'Abbas read: "fa-man ya'tikum bi-ma'in 'adhb" (sweet water).

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿Is one who walks prostrate⟩ that he said: "In error." ﴿Or one who walks upright⟩: "Rightly guided."

al-Khatib in his History and Ibn al-Najjar related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever has a toothache, let him place his finger on it and recite this verse: ﴿He it is who brought you into being and made for you hearing, sight and hearts; little is it that you give thanks﴾."

al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever has a toothache, let him place his finger on it, and let him recite these two verses seven times: ﴿And He it is who brought you into being from a single soul, so there is a place of settlement and a place of storage﴾ up to ﴿they understand﴾ [al-An'am: 98], and ﴿He it is who brought you into being and made for you hearing, sight and hearts; little is it that you give thanks﴾, for it will be healed by Allah's permission."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿If your water should become sunken﴾ that he said: "Entering into the earth." ﴿Then who will bring you clear water?⟩ He said: "The flowing."

Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him: ﴿If your water should become sunken⟩, he said: "It returns into the earth." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him, regarding ﴿clear water⟩, that he said: "Apparent."

Abd ibn Humayd also related from him, regarding ﴿clear water⟩: "Sweet."

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Muhaysin read it with ishmam. ﴿And it will be said: This is what you used to call for⟩, meaning: it is said to them as reproach and rebuke: this visible, present punishment is the punishment that you used to call for in the world, meaning you were seeking it and hastening it in mockery, on the basis that the meaning of "tad'un" is "du'a" (calling/supplicating).

Al-Farra' said: "tadda'una" is from "du'a", meaning: you wish for it and ask for it, and most exegetes said this.

Al-Zajjaj said: "This is what you used to claim" refers to the falsehoods and tales.

It was also said: the meaning of "tadda'un" is "you lie." This is on the recitation of the majority, "tadda'un" with shaddah, so it is either from "du'a" as most said, or from "da'wa" (claim) as al-Zajjaj and those who agreed with him said, and the meaning is: they used to claim that there is no resurrection, no gathering, no Paradise and no Fire.

Qatadah and Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ya'qub and al-Dahhak read "tad'un" without shaddah, and its meaning is clear.

Qatadah said: it is their saying: ﴿Our Lord, hasten for us our portion﴾ [Sad: 16]. Al-Dahhak said: it is their saying: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], the verse.

Al-Nahhas said: "tadda'un" and "tad'un" have one meaning, as you say "qadara" and "iqtadara", and "ghada" and "ightada", except that "af'ala" means it passed one thing after another, while "fi'l" applies to the few and the many.

﴿Say: Have you considered, if Allah destroys me and those with me⟩, meaning: inform me, if Allah destroys me and those with me by punishment, or has mercy on us and does not punish us, ﴿then who will protect the disbelievers from a painful punishment?⟩, meaning: who will protect them and secure them from the punishment.

The meaning is: none will save them from that, whether Allah destroys His Messenger and the believers with him, as the disbelievers were wishing, or grants them respite.

It was also said: the meaning is: we, with our faith, are between fear and hope, so who will protect you, with your disbelief, from the punishment? The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun in order to brand them with disbelief and to show that it is the cause of their not being saved.

﴿Say: He is the Most Merciful; we have believed in Him⟩ alone, we associate nothing with Him, ﴿and upon Him we have relied⟩ and not upon anyone else.

Tawakkul is committing affairs to Him, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿So you will know who is in clear error⟩, we or you.

In this is a severe threat, with the speech presented in the manner of fairness.

The majority read "sata'lamun" with the second person (ta). Al-Kisa'i read it with the third person (ya), as a report.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, argued against them with some of His blessings, and made them fear the removal of that blessing from them, so He said: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should become sunken⟩, meaning: inform me, if your water becomes absorbed into the earth so that no trace of it remains in it at all, or it goes away into the earth to a far place so that buckets cannot reach it.

It is said: "ghaara al-ma'u ghawran," meaning it receded. "Al-ghawr" is the sunken, described by a verbal noun for emphasis, as one says "rajul 'adl" (a just man). A similar case has already been mentioned in Surat al-Kahf. ﴿Then who will bring you clear water?⟩, meaning apparent water that eyes can see and buckets can reach. It was also said: it is from "ma'ana al-ma'u", meaning it became abundant.

Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: it means flowing. The meaning of "ma'in" has already been mentioned in Surat al-Mu'min.

Ibn 'Abbas read: "fa-man ya'tikum bi-ma'in 'adhb" (sweet water).

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿Is one who walks prostrate⟩ that he said: "In error." ﴿Or one who walks upright⟩: "Rightly guided."

al-Khatib in his History and Ibn al-Najjar related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever has a toothache, let him place his finger on it and recite this verse: ﴿He it is who brought you into being and made for you hearing, sight and hearts; little is it that you give thanks﴾."

al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever has a toothache, let him place his finger on it, and let him recite these two verses seven times: ﴿And He it is who brought you into being from a single soul, so there is a place of settlement and a place of storage﴾ up to ﴿they understand﴾ [al-An'am: 98], and ﴿He it is who brought you into being and made for you hearing, sight and hearts; little is it that you give thanks﴾, for it will be healed by Allah's permission."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿If your water should become sunken﴾ that he said: "Entering into the earth." ﴿Then who will bring you clear water?⟩ He said: "The flowing."

Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him: ﴿If your water should become sunken⟩, he said: "It returns into the earth." Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also related from him, regarding ﴿clear water⟩, that he said: "Apparent."

Abd ibn Humayd also related from him, regarding ﴿clear water⟩: "Sweet."
